purpose: Assess whether an GCP delivery team can implement the proposed design and whether four audiences can understand and challenge it. This is an LLM-assisted critique, not a deployment certification. Judge the actual PDF and diagrams, not author confidence or document length. A high communication score cannot cancel a deployment blocker.

personas.perspective: A developer with basic HTTP, database and cloud knowledge but no knowledge of this system. Can this reader explain one complete numbered journey, identify where to implement each responsibility, find configuration and tests, understand unfamiliar terms, and follow a denied or failed request? Penalize unexplained acronyms, contradictory arrows and implementation gaps hidden behind product names.

An accountable technology executive. Can this reader identify the business outcome, deployment feasibility, isolation model, alternatives, recurring cost drivers, staffing/operational burden, service/recovery commitments and decisions requiring approval? Penalize false precision, unsupported availability and cost claims, and executive summaries that hide blockers.

An external GCP enterprise architect asked to hand the design to a delivery team. Trace projects, ownership, specific hosting/tier/region support, capacity, networking/DNS, interfaces, durable state, deployment/bootstrap order, compatibility and migration. Seek contradictions between model, diagram and text. Missing deployability details are major findings even when the narrative reads well. Check current GCP primary sources for consequential suspect claims and cite them in the critique.

An external security architect conducting an adversarial design review. Trace human and workload identity, SSO tenant binding, authorization and revocation, network trust boundaries, private routing/DNS/egress, provider support and deployment access, customer isolation, key custody, data residency/lifecycle, audit and AI/tool threats. Challenge customer-to-customer access, shared control-plane compromise, prompt injection and unsafe retries. Distinguish proposed control, enforcement mechanism and executed evidence; do not accept compliance or tested recovery by assertion.

anchors.1: Contradictory or unreadable; key responsibilities and flows cannot be identified.
anchors.2: Readable in places but ambiguous labels, undefined terms or inconsistent diagrams obstruct review.
anchors.3: Main decisions and flows are clear; localized explanations or labels still need work.
anchors.4: Precise, well-structured and consistent across narrative, diagrams and flow tables; risks are explicit.
anchors.5: Immediately navigable at each audience's depth; precise references, legible views and explanations resolve likely misunderstandings without hiding trade-offs.

anchors.1: Material requirements are omitted or the design is implausibly overbuilt; complexity hides correctness failures.
anchors.2: Important distributed behavior is hand-waved or unnecessary services obscure a deployable design.
anchors.3: Complexity mostly matches requirements, with documented responsibilities but some avoidable coupling or gaps.
anchors.4: Every material service/boundary is justified; concurrency, failure, operation and migration are explained with realistic alternatives.
anchors.5: The smallest credible design handles the stated scale and failures; complexity is partitioned into readable views with explicit operational cost and limits. This is complexity management, not a reward for more services.

anchors.1: This persona cannot explain the design or act on it without reconstructing it.
anchors.2: This persona understands the idea but must invent important deployment, decision or review details.
anchors.3: This persona can explain the main journey and act on most of its responsibilities, with identifiable follow-up questions.
anchors.4: This persona can independently trace normal/failure behavior and use the pack for implementation, funding or architectural/security review.
anchors.5: This persona can accurately teach or challenge the design using the pack alone; concrete settings, diagrams, evidence, ownership and acceptance tests make remaining uncertainty bounded and actionable.

reviewProtocol: Read the cumulative input and inspect every actual PDF page and every SVG at readable scale. Record exact pages and nodes. Text extraction helps find claims but does not establish visual inspection. Missing or uninspectable artifacts produce blocked, not pass.

Apply each persona separately. Include strengths and actionable findings with path and page/node evidence. Do not inflate scores because the author used Atlas GCP, official icons, many pages or a successful assembler command.

Grade every cumulative acceptance item met, partial or unmet. Deployment realism is a hard gate: unsupported service/tier/network combinations, absent authorization enforcement, unowned durable state, missing bootstrap/deployment dependencies or unresolved contradictions must be partial/unmet and major/critical as appropriate.

Required cloud feasibility checks may legitimately remain unexecuted in this non-deploying benchmark if the design is concrete, evidence-grounded and names exact verification steps. Do not punish honest untested targets as if tested deployment were in scope; do punish claims of deployment readiness that conceal unresolved feasibility.

Critical means plausible cross-customer compromise, destructive/unsafe execution, residency violation or an impossible critical path. Major means a delivery/review blocker or a material requirement gap. Minor means localized wording/layout or a nonblocking omission.
Compare earlier frozen artifacts for loss of requirements, unexplained service changes and renumbering; cite regression findings. Evaluate the cumulative output, not only its delta.

Pass requires all 12 persona scores at least 4, every acceptance item met, no critical/major findings and zero regressions, including minor regressions. Record every regression in regressionFindings regardless of severity. A higher score cannot offset a score below 4. Scores are ordinal judgments, not calibrated measurements. One independent context applying four personas is not four independent experts or model diversity. Report the runtime identity when available and never invent the model identity. This single-run evaluation cannot establish statistical reliability or causal benefit over a no-skill control.
